content: In 1951, D. Roberts discussed the properties of cyclobutyl cations, but the actual ions were first described by S. Winstein in 1949 to explain the reactivity of certain norbornyl compounds. The compounds in question are exo-norbornyl brosylate (compound 1) and its endo isomer (compound 3), as shown in Scheme 1. The reaction involves solvolysis or acylation using the potassium salt of acetic acid in acetic acid. A critical observation is that, in this nucleophilic displacement reaction, both isomers yield the same reaction product, an exo-acetate (compound 2). Additionally, the reaction rate for the exo isomer is 350 times faster than that of the endo isomer or a cyclohexyl control reaction. In a related experiment, both enantiomers of the exo-brosylate (compounds 1 and 2) undergo solvolysis to produce the same racemic reaction product, as shown in Scheme 2. The optical activity of the reaction disappears at the same rate as the solvolysis reaction. These findings are explained by the formation of a non-classical ion (compound 3 in Scheme 3) as a reactive intermediate. This ion is the initial reaction product of both the endo (compound 1) and exo (compound 2) isomers. The ion forms when sigma electrons in the C1-C6 bond participate via neighboring group assistance, facilitating the expulsion of the leaving group. The positive charge initially localized on C1 becomes delocalized onto C2 as well. The formation of this carbocation is the slow, rate-determining step of the reaction. In this step, the exo leaving group is better positioned relative to C1 than the endo leaving group, which explains the significant difference in reactivity. The intermediate ion features a pentavalent C2 carbon atom, classifying it as a carbonium ion. The ion is also symmetrical, a property more apparent in the equivalent structure 3b. This symmetry accounts for the observed racemization. The ion carries a full positive charge distributed across C2, C6, and C7. Further evidence for this model was obtained through tracer studies, where two carbon atoms in the norbornyl skeleton were replaced with radioactive carbon-14 isotopes (Scheme 4). The primary solvolysis reaction product was derivatized by reduction with lithium aluminum hydride and oxidation with sodium permanganate to form a dicarboxylic acid, followed by a Curtius rearrangement that expelled carbon dioxide. If the acetyl anion can attack both the C1 and C2 positions of the symmetrical norbornyl cation (compound 2), then 50% of the generated CO2 would contain carbon-14. The experimental value was 40%, and to account for the presence of carbon-14 in other positions (due to a scrambling process), the nortricyclonium cation was proposed. This cation is essentially a face-capped norbornyl cation that allows hydride shifts. In 1964, George A. Olah provided direct evidence for the norbornyl cation. He subjected the norbornyl antimony chloropentafluoride salt, obtained by reacting exo-2-chloro-norbornane with antimony pentafluoride, to NMR analysis. At room temperature, the NMR spectrum showed a single broad peak due to hydride shifts. However, these shifts could be partially frozen when cooled to -60°C in liquid sulfur dioxide. It was also discovered that the norbornyl cation could be generated from norbornanes with chlorine substituents at the bridging or bridgehead positions, as well as from the reaction of norbornene with HSbF6. These findings confirmed the rearrangements occurring in the carbon-14 scrambling process. Solid-state NMR analysis was conducted at temperatures as low as 5 kelvins, where all positions are assumed to be frozen. One of the two signals visible in the spectrum corresponded to the identical C1 and C2 carbon atoms.
